title: Summarising Data
subtitle: Counting, totalling and averaging — turning thousands of rows into one useful number.

lessons.title: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
lessons.summary: The five functions that squeeze a whole column down into a single answer.
lessons.examTip: COUNT counts rows, SUM adds a column, AVG averages it, MIN finds the smallest and MAX the largest. They are called aggregate functions because they work on a whole group of rows at once.

steps.title: One number instead of a thousand rows
steps.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS number_of_students
FROM students;
steps.expect: One row, one column, one number — six.

lines.text: Everything we have done so far has given us rows. Lists of students, lists of courses.
But the principal does not want a list. She wants a number.
How many students do we have? What is the total fees collected? What is the average?
For that we use aggregate functions. Aggregate simply means, work out one answer for a whole group.
The first one is COUNT. So we write COUNT, and then star in brackets.
COUNT star means, count the rows, all of them.
And I am giving it an alias, AS number_of_students, so the heading is readable.
Always give an aggregate an alias. Without one the heading is ugly and the marker cannot tell what you calculated.
Run.
Look at that.
One row. One column. The number six.
Six students. It did not show me the students. It counted them and gave me the answer.
That is the big idea of this chapter. Many rows go in, one number comes out.

marks.cue: And I am giving it an alias, AS number_of_students

steps.title: SUM and AVG
steps.expect: The total fees collected, and the average per student.

lines.text: Now the bursar's two questions. How much money have we collected, and what is the average payment?
Watch the two functions.
SUM, brackets, fees_paid. That adds up every value in that column.
AVG, brackets, fees_paid. That works out the average.
And notice, this time I do not put a star inside the brackets. I put a column name.
That is an important difference. You can count rows, but you cannot add up rows. You add up a column.
So COUNT takes a star. SUM and AVG must be given a numeric column.
And notice I asked for two functions in one SELECT, separated by a comma. That is allowed, and it is efficient.
Run.
There are the bursar's numbers.
Two thousand two hundred and forty six dollars and fifty cents, collected in total.
And the average is about three hundred and seventy four dollars per student.
Now, one thing about AVG that the exam likes to test.
AVG ignores NULL values completely. It does not count them as zero. It leaves them out of the calculation altogether.
So if some students had no fee record at all, the average would be worked out on the others only. Remember that.

steps.title: MIN and MAX
steps.sql:
SELECT MIN(fees_paid) AS smallest_payment,
       MAX(fees_paid) AS largest_payment,
       COUNT(*) AS number_of_students
FROM students;
steps.expect: The smallest payment, the largest payment, and the number of students, all in one row.

lines.text: Two more, and then you have all five.
MIN gives you the smallest value in a column. MAX gives you the largest.
So MIN and MAX, each with the column in brackets.
And I am putting COUNT in the same query, so you can see how they sit together.
Run.
Look at the row.
The smallest payment is zero. That is Farai, who has paid nothing.
The largest is one thousand two hundred and fifty dollars and seventy five cents. That is Kuda.
And six students in the college.
Now here is a trap, and I have seen it catch many students, so listen.
You might think, let me add first_name to that SELECT, so I can see who paid the most.
Do not do it. A plain name is one row, but MAX is one answer for the whole table. They do not fit together.
The right way to find who paid the most is the one we learned in Chapter Four.
ORDER BY fees_paid DESC, LIMIT one. Sort them and take the top one.
MIN and MAX give you the value. ORDER BY and LIMIT give you the person.

marks.cue: So MIN and MAX, each with the column in brackets
And I am putting COUNT in the same query

steps.title: Aggregates with a WHERE
steps.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS it_students,
       SUM(fees_paid) AS it_money
FROM students
WHERE programme = 'NC IT';
steps.expect: The count and total for NC IT only — four students.

lines.text: One more thing before the next lesson, and it is simpler than you expect.
An aggregate is still a SELECT. So everything you already know still works.
How many students are in NC IT, and how much have they paid between them?
So we just add WHERE, exactly as before.
COUNT star, SUM of fees_paid, FROM students, WHERE programme equals NC IT.
The WHERE runs first. It picks the rows. Then the aggregate works on whatever survived.
Filter first, then count. That is the order, and it never changes.
Run.
Four IT students.
And two thousand one hundred and seventy one dollars and twenty five cents between them.
Now, that is useful. But what if the principal wants that for every programme, not just IT?
Do we write the query three times, once for each programme? No. That is the next lesson.

marks.cue: COUNT star, SUM of fees_paid, FROM students, WHERE programme equals NC IT

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: Aggregate questions are short and they are free marks if you have practised them.
First, know the definition. An aggregate function performs a calculation on a set of values and returns a single value.
Then know the five, and what each one takes.
COUNT star counts rows. SUM of a column adds them. AVG of a column averages them. MIN and MAX find the extremes.
Watch out for the English in the question, because it tells you which one they want.
How many means COUNT. Total means SUM. Average or mean means AVG. Highest or most means MAX. Lowest, cheapest or least means MIN.
And always, always give it an alias with AS. It costs you three seconds and it makes your answer look professional.
One last one they like. What is the difference between COUNT star and COUNT of a column name?
COUNT star counts all the rows. COUNT of a column counts only the rows where that column is not NULL.

items.text: An aggregate function performs a calculation on a set of values and returns a single value.

points: Counts only rows where that column is not NULL

lessons.title: GROUP BY and HAVING
lessons.summary: One answer per category instead of one answer for the whole table.
lessons.examTip: GROUP BY splits rows into groups and applies the aggregate to each group. HAVING filters those groups. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. That difference is the exam question.

steps.title: One answer per group
steps.expect: One row per programme, each with its own count.

lines.text: In the last lesson we counted the whole college, and we counted IT on its own.
But the principal wants a breakdown. How many in each programme, all on one page.
Now, we could write the query three times and change the WHERE each time. But that is slow, and if a new programme starts you would miss it.
So instead we tell the database to split the rows into piles, and count each pile.
Look at the last line.
GROUP BY programme.
Picture what that does. It takes all seven students and puts them into piles, one pile per programme.
The IT pile. The Accounting pile. The Marketing pile.
And then COUNT star runs once inside each pile, not once for the whole table.
Run.
There is the breakdown.
NC IT, four learners. NC Accounting, two. NC Marketing, one.
Three rows, one for each pile. And it added up to seven, which is everybody.
Now look at the SELECT line again, because there is a rule hiding in it.
I asked for programme, and I asked for COUNT star. Nothing else.
The rule is this. Anything in your SELECT that is not inside an aggregate function must also be in the GROUP BY.
You cannot ask for first_name here. Which of the four IT names would it show you? The question makes no sense.
So: grouped column, and aggregates. That is all that may go in the SELECT.

marks.cue: I asked for programme, and I asked for COUNT star

steps.title: More than one number per group
steps.sql:
SELECT programme,
       COUNT(*) AS learners,
       SUM(fees_paid) AS money_collected,
       AVG(fees_paid) AS average_payment
FROM students
GROUP BY programme
ORDER BY money_collected DESC;
steps.expect: A full management report — count, total and average for every programme.

lines.text: Now we can build a real management report, and it takes almost no extra effort.
Watch how much information I get from six lines.
The programme, the number of learners, the money collected, and the average payment.
All grouped by programme, and then sorted by money, biggest first.
And look where the ORDER BY is. Right at the bottom, after the GROUP BY.
That is the order we recited in Chapter Four. SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
Run.
Now look at that. That is a report a principal would actually use.
NC IT is at the top with four learners and over two thousand dollars.
NC Accounting has two learners and four hundred and eighty dollars.
And NC Marketing, one learner and seventy five dollars.
Look at the average column too. It tells a different story from the total.
A programme can collect a lot of money simply because it has many students. The average shows you how each individual is doing.
That is the difference between data and information. We had data. Now we have information.

marks.cue: And look where the ORDER BY is

steps.title: HAVING — filtering the groups
steps.sql:
SELECT programme, COUNT(*) AS learners
FROM students
GROUP BY programme
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
steps.expect: Only the programmes with more than one learner. Marketing disappears.

lines.text: Now the last piece of SQL in this course, and it is the one students find confusing. Let me make it simple.
The principal says, only show me the programmes that have more than one learner.
Now your instinct will be to reach for WHERE. And WHERE will not work here. Let me explain why.
WHERE runs before the grouping. At that moment there are no groups yet, and there is no count yet.
You cannot filter on a count that has not been calculated. The database has not done the counting when WHERE runs.
So we need a filter that runs afterwards, once the piles have been counted.
So we use HAVING.
HAVING COUNT star greater than one.
HAVING is the WHERE clause for groups. That is the sentence to remember.
And it sits after the GROUP BY, never before it.
Run.
Two rows now.
NC IT with four, and NC Accounting with two.
NC Marketing had only one learner, so its whole group was thrown out of the answer.
Notice what got filtered. Not a student. A whole group.
WHERE throws away rows. HAVING throws away groups. That is the whole difference.

marks.cue: HAVING COUNT star greater than one

steps.title: Using WHERE and HAVING together
steps.sql:
SELECT programme, COUNT(*) AS paying_learners
FROM students
WHERE fees_paid > 0
GROUP BY programme
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
steps.expect: Only NC IT survives — it is the one programme with more than one paying learner.

lines.text: And now let us put them both in one query, because that is where it finally clicks.
The question is: which programmes have more than one learner who has actually paid something?
Read it from the top with me, line by line.
WHERE fees_paid greater than zero. That runs first, and it throws away Farai, who has paid nothing.
GROUP BY programme. That runs second, and it puts the survivors into piles.
HAVING COUNT star greater than one. That runs third, and it throws away any pile that is too small.
Filter the rows. Make the piles. Filter the piles. Three steps, in that order, every time.
Run.
One row. NC IT, four paying learners.
Accounting lost Farai to the WHERE, so it only had one paying learner left, and then HAVING removed the whole group.
Marketing only ever had one, so it was removed too.
One query answered a question that would take you an hour with a calculator and a printed list.
That is what SQL is for.

marks.cue: GROUP BY programme. That runs second
HAVING COUNT star greater than one. That runs third

steps.title: How this looks in the exam

lines.text: This is one of the most reliable questions on the paper, so let us nail it.
The question. Differentiate between the WHERE clause and the HAVING clause.
Answer. WHERE filters individual records before they are grouped, and it cannot be used with aggregate functions.
HAVING filters groups after the grouping has taken place, and it is used with aggregate functions.
Before and after. Rows and groups. Those two contrasts are the marks.
And in a practical question, when you see the words for each, or per, that is your GROUP BY signal.
The number of students for each programme. Total sales per branch. Average mark per subject. All GROUP BY.
And when you see only those groups with, or where the count is more than, that is HAVING.
For each means GROUP BY. Only those groups means HAVING. Two phrases, two clauses.
